content: Bowen's disease is also referred to as Bowen's carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the skin, intraepidermal carcinoma of the skin, or intraepithelial neoplasia. In the field of dermatology, Bowen's disease (BD) is recognized as a skin condition primarily induced by prolonged exposure to sunlight. It is classified as an early, noninvasive stage or an intraepidermal form of squamous cell carcinoma. If left undiagnosed, untreated, or neglected, there is less than a 10% chance that it may progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the skin. Clinically, Bowen's disease typically presents as an erythematous (reddened), scaly, or crusty patch or plaque. While it can occur anywhere on the body, it most commonly affects the lower legs. Other potential sites of involvement include the head, neck, genital region, and skin folds. The condition is highly treatable and can be effectively managed through various therapeutic approaches. These include cryotherapy (freezing the lesion), curettage (scraping the lesion), cautery (burning the lesion), photodynamic therapy (using light-activated drugs), topical chemotherapy (application of anti-cancer medications), radiotherapy (radiation treatment), or surgical excision of the lesion. In 1912, Dr. John T. Bowen first described this condition, which has since been named after him.
